claim: In the vertebrate central nervous system, groups of functionally related neurons, including cranial motor neurons of the brainstem, are frequently organised as nuclei.
source: In the vertebrate central nervous system, groups of functionally related neurons, including cranial motor neurons of the brainstem, are frequently organised as nuclei.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about neuronal organization in the CNS.

claim: Developing ocular motor (sub)nuclei differentially express classical cadherins.
source: We find that developing ocular motor (sub)nuclei differentially express classical cadherins.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAscope in situ hybridization data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Perturbing cadherin function in ocular motor neurons results in distinct defects in neuronal positioning, including scattering of dorsal cells and defective contralateral migration of ventral subnuclei.
source: Perturbing cadherin function in these neurons results in distinct defects in neuronal positioning, including scattering of dorsal cells and defective contralateral migration of ventral subnuclei.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using the cdh2ΔEC transgenic line shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Cadherin-mediated interactions between adjacent subnuclei are critical for subnucleus position.
source: In addition, we show that cadherin-mediated interactions between adjacent subnuclei are critical for subnucleus position.
evidence: This claim is supported by data on IO neuron positioning shown in Figure 5.

claim: Disrupting cadherin adhesivity in dorsal oculomotor neurons impairs the larval optokinetic reflex.
source: We also find that disrupting cadherin adhesivity in dorsal oculomotor neurons impairs the larval optokinetic reflex, suggesting that neuronal clustering is important for co-ordinating circuit function.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 7.

claim: The correct arrangement of motor neurons within nuclei is thought to be critical for multiple aspects of circuit formation, including muscle target innervation and acquisition of sensory inputs.
source: The correct arrangement of motor neurons within nuclei is thought to be critical for multiple aspects of circuit formation, including muscle target innervation and acquisition of sensory inputs (Landmesser, 1978; Sürmeli et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Some cranial motor nuclei, such as the oculomotor nucleus and facial motor nucleus, can be further divided into subnuclei according to their efferent projections.
source: In the brainstem, some cranial motor nuclei, such as the oculomotor nucleus and facial motor nucleus, can be further divided into subnuclei according to their efferent projections.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about brainstem organization.

claim: Neurons that contribute axons to the same cranial nerve yet innervate different muscle targets exhibit stereotyped topography within the larger nucleus.
source: Neurons that contribute axons to the same cranial nerve yet innervate different muscle targets exhibit stereotyped topography within the larger nucleus (Greaney et al., 2017; McArthur and Fetcho, 2017; Barsh et al., 2017; Isabella et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The positioning of some groups of motor neurons has been shown to be regulated by members of the classical cadherin superfamily of cell adhesion molecules.
source: The positioning of some groups of motor neurons has been shown to be regulated by members of the classical cadherin superfamily of cell adhesion molecules, which include type I and type II cadherins (Price et al., 2002; Demireva et al., 2011; Astick et al., 2014; Dewitz et al., 2018; Dewitz et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Type II cadherins participate in homophilic as well as heterophilic interactions.
source: Differential expression of type II cadherins, which participate in homophilic as well as heterophilic interactions (Patel et al., 2006), drives the segregation and coalescence of somatomotor and branchiomotor neurons into discrete cranial motor nuclei in the hindbrain (Astick et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Patel et al., 2006.

claim: Differential expression of type II cadherins drives the segregation and coalescence of somatomotor and branchiomotor neurons into discrete cranial motor nuclei in the hindbrain.
source: Differential expression of type II cadherins, which participate in homophilic as well as heterophilic interactions (Patel et al., 2006), drives the segregation and coalescence of somatomotor and branchiomotor neurons into discrete cranial motor nuclei in the hindbrain (Astick et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Astick et al., 2014.

claim: Cadherins participate in an intricate network of interactions with gap junctions and spontaneous activity to regulate the emergence of mature topography in brainstem motor nuclei.
source: Furthermore, cadherins participate in an intricate network of interactions with gap junctions and spontaneous activity, to regulate the emergence of mature topography in brainstem motor nuclei (Montague et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Montague et al., 2017.

claim: The zebrafish ocular motor system comprises the oculomotor nucleus (nIII) of the midbrain, as well as the trochlear (nIV) and abducens nuclei (nVI) of the hindbrain.
source: The zebrafish ocular motor system, which comprises the oculomotor nucleus (nIII) of the midbrain, as well as the trochlear (nIV) and abducens nuclei (nVI) of the hindbrain, provides an unparalleled opportunity to address these questions.
evidence: This is a description of the anatomical organization of the zebrafish ocular motor system.

claim: The anatomical layout of the zebrafish ocular motor system is well-conserved among vertebrates.
source: The anatomical layout of the system is well-conserved among vertebrates; together the three nuclei innervate six extraocular muscles responsible for coordinating important eye movements (Graf and McGurk, 1985; Evinger, 1988; Gilland and Baker, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to comparative anatomy studies.

claim: The three ocular motor nuclei together innervate six extraocular muscles responsible for coordinating important eye movements.
source: The anatomical layout of the system is well-conserved among vertebrates; together the three nuclei innervate six extraocular muscles responsible for coordinating important eye movements (Graf and McGurk, 1985; Evinger, 1988; Gilland and Baker, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations describing the functional anatomy.

claim: Four extraocular muscles are innervated by the four constituent subnuclei of nIII.
source: Four of these muscles are innervated by the four constituent subnuclei of nIII, whereas nIV and nVI each target a single muscle.
evidence: This is a description of the innervation pattern of the oculomotor nucleus.

claim: Oculomotor subnuclei exhibit spatial topography with respect to muscle target, segregated along the dorsoventral axis.
source: Oculomotor subnuclei are known to exhibit spatial topography with respect to muscle target, segregated along the dorsoventral axis (Greaney et al., 2017);
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Greaney et al., 2017.

claim: In higher vertebrates, the Edinger-Westphal nucleus is located dorsal to nIII.
source: in higher vertebrates, this organisation also extends to the visceral motor neurons of the Edinger-Westphal nucleus which is located dorsal to nIII (Hasan et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hasan et al., 2010.

claim: Neurons belonging to the superior rectus (SR) subnucleus translocate their soma across the midline in an unusual migration to the contralateral side.
source: Curiously, neurons belonging to the superior rectus (SR) subnucleus translocate their soma across the midline in an unusual migration to the contralateral side (Puelles-Lopez et al., 1975; Naujoks-Manteuffel et al., 1991), giving rise to contralateral connectivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies describing SR neuron migration.

claim: Cadherins control distinct aspects of cranial motor neuron positioning, including the clustering of neurons belonging to dorsal oculomotor subnuclei and the contralateral migration of ventral SR neurons.
source: We demonstrate that cadherins control distinct aspects of cranial motor neuron positioning, including the clustering of neurons belonging to dorsal oculomotor subnuclei and the contralateral migration of ventral SR neurons, while also regulating subnuclear position through adhesive interactions between constituent oculomotor subnuclei.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by experimental data presented in Figures 2, 3, and 5.

claim: Eye movements driven by oculomotor neurons in which clustering is perturbed are defective.
source: In addition, we find that eye movements driven by oculomotor neurons in which clustering is perturbed are defective, raising the possibility that their assembly into nuclei is important for circuit function.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data in Figure 7.

claim: Recent work indicates that type II cadherins act synergistically with the type I cadherin cdh2 (N-Cadherin) to control motor neuron positioning.
source: In addition to their established roles in controlling motor neuron topography (Price et al., 2002; Astick et al., 2014), recent work indicates that type II cadherins act synergistically with the type I cadherin cdh2 (N-Cadherin) to control their precise positioning, although the exact mechanism remains unclear (Dewitz et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dewitz et al., 2019.

claim: In transgenic Isl1:GFP zebrafish embryos, the majority of ocular motor neurons, including trochlear (nIV) and most oculomotor (nIII) neurons express GFP.
source: Cadherin transcript detection was performed in transgenic Isl1:GFP zebrafish embryos, in which the majority of ocular motor neurons, including trochlear (nIV) and most oculomotor (nIII) neurons are known to express GFP (Higashijima et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Higashijima et al., 2000.

claim: nIII neurons innervating the inferior oblique (IO) muscle lack GFP expression in Isl1:GFP transgenic zebrafish.
source: nIII neurons innervating the inferior oblique (IO) muscle, as well as abducens (nVI) motor neurons, lack GFP expression;
evidence: This is a description of the expression pattern in the transgenic line.

claim: Abducens (nVI) motor neurons lack GFP expression in Isl1:GFP transgenic zebrafish.
source: nIII neurons innervating the inferior oblique (IO) muscle, as well as abducens (nVI) motor neurons, lack GFP expression;
evidence: This is a description of the expression pattern in the transgenic line.

claim: Ocular motor neurons display a fanned arrangement during development within the intact brain.
source: Isl1:GFP fluorescence was preserved following RNAscope processing, allowing expression of individual mRNAs to be examined in ocular motor neurons, which display a fanned arrangement during development, within the intact brain (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: nIII neurons are generated and distributed along the dorsoventral (DV) axis stereotypically.
source: Due to the lack of subpopulation-specific markers, expression in nIII subnuclei was assayed based on their anatomical location, as neurons are generated and distributed along the dorsoventral (DV) axis stereotypically (Greaney et al., 2017; Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Greaney et al., 2017 and Figure 1B-C.

claim: The dorsal portion of nIII contains motor neuron groups innervating the inferior rectus (IR) and medial rectus (MR) muscles.
source: Whereas the dorsal portion of nIII contains motor neuron groups innervating the inferior rectus (IR) and medial rectus (MR) muscles, ventral (and medial) nIII predominantly contains superior rectus (SR)-innervating neurons, as well as inferior oblique (IO) neurons just lateral to these (Greaney et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Greaney et al., 2017.

claim: Ventral (and medial) nIII predominantly contains superior rectus (SR)-innervating neurons, as well as inferior oblique (IO) neurons just lateral to these.
source: Whereas the dorsal portion of nIII contains motor neuron groups innervating the inferior rectus (IR) and medial rectus (MR) muscles, ventral (and medial) nIII predominantly contains superior rectus (SR)-innervating neurons, as well as inferior oblique (IO) neurons just lateral to these (Greaney et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Greaney et al., 2017.

claim: IO neurons are found further dorsal in zebrafish, consistent with reports in other teleost species.
source: Our data indicate that IO neurons are also found further dorsal, consistent with reports in other teleost species (Graf and McGurk, 1985; Luiten and de Vlieger, 1978).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in the study and citations to previous reports.

claim: Superior oblique (SO)-innervating neurons belonging to nIV are located proximal to and just rostral of nIII in rhombomere 1 (r1) of the hindbrain.
source: Superior oblique (SO)-innervating neurons belonging to nIV are located proximal to and just rostral of nIII in rhombomere 1 (r1) of the hindbrain.
evidence: This is a description of the anatomical location of nIV neurons.

claim: At 48 hpf, ocular motor neurons expressed combinations of cadherins.
source: At 48 hpf, ocular motor neurons expressed combinations of cadherins (Figure 1B–L; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D and F–G), and differential expression was observed between dorsal and ventral nIII subnuclei, as well as between nIII and nIV.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAscope data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Differential cadherin expression was observed between dorsal and ventral nIII subnuclei, as well as between nIII and nIV at 48 hpf.
source: At 48 hpf, ocular motor neurons expressed combinations of cadherins (Figure 1B–L; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D and F–G), and differential expression was observed between dorsal and ventral nIII subnuclei, as well as between nIII and nIV.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAscope data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Detection of cadherin mRNA by RNAscope was highly specific, as in situ hybridisation with a negative control probe against the bacterial mRNA dapB revealed almost no signal.
source: Detection was highly specific, as in situ hybridisation with a negative control probe against the bacterial mRNA dapB revealed almost no signal (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and E),
evidence: This claim is supported by negative control data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and E.

claim: Expression of the transcription factor foxg1a within the CNS was restricted to telencephalic regions consistent with its known expression pattern.
source: whereas expression of the transcription factor foxg1a within the CNS was restricted to telencephalic regions consistent with its known expression pattern (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Danesin et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by positive control data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and a citation to Danesin et al., 2009.

claim: Selectivity of adhesion between cell types can be achieved by discrete profiles of cadherin expression, as well as by varying levels of the same cadherin.
source: Previous work has shown that selectivity of adhesion between cell types can be achieved by discrete profiles of cadherin expression, as well as by varying levels of the same cadherin (Price et al., 2002; Steinberg and Takeichi, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cadherin expression within ocular motor (sub)nuclei and surrounding non-motor neuron cell types varies both in intensity and spatial distribution.
source: We find that cadherin expression within ocular motor (sub)nuclei and surrounding non-motor neuron cell types varies both in intensity and spatial distribution.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: Expression of the type I cadherin cdh2 (N-Cadherin) was detected in all ocular motor neurons, displaying a broad and relatively uniform distribution across subnuclei.
source: For example, expression of the type I cadherin cdh2 (N-Cadherin) and type II cadherin cdh11 was detected in all ocular motor neurons, displaying a broad and relatively uniform distribution across subnuclei, as well as cells immediately surrounding them, with cdh2 displaying the highest levels of expression of all surveyed cadherins (Figure 1D, H and L; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAscope data shown in Figure 1D, H and L.

claim: Expression of type II cadherin cdh11 was detected in all ocular motor neurons, displaying a broad and relatively uniform distribution across subnuclei.
source: For example, expression of the type I cadherin cdh2 (N-Cadherin) and type II cadherin cdh11 was detected in all ocular motor neurons, displaying a broad and relatively uniform distribution across subnuclei, as well as cells immediately surrounding them, with cdh2 displaying the highest levels of expression of all surveyed cadherins (Figure 1D, H and L; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAscope data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and G.

claim: cdh2 displayed the highest levels of expression of all surveyed cadherins in ocular motor neurons at 48 hpf.
source: For example, expression of the type I cadherin cdh2 (N-Cadherin) and type II cadherin cdh11 was detected in all ocular motor neurons, displaying a broad and relatively uniform distribution across subnuclei, as well as cells immediately surrounding them, with cdh2 displaying the highest levels of expression of all surveyed cadherins (Figure 1D, H and L; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: GFP-negative IO neurons are likely to express cdh2 and cdh11, in addition to GFP-expressing ocular motor neurons.
source: Based on anatomical location, GFP-negative IO neurons are therefore also likely to express cdh2 and cdh11, in addition to GFP-expressing ocular motor neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the broad expression pattern of cdh2 and cdh11 and the anatomical location of IO neurons.

claim: Dorsal nIII subnuclei expressed cdh4 (type I), which exhibited negligible expression in ventromedial nIII.
source: Dorsal subnuclei expressed several cadherins, including cdh4 (type I; Figure 1E, I and L) and cdh10a (type II; Figure 1G, K and L), which exhibited negligible expression in ventromedial nIII.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAscope data shown in Figure 1E, I and L.

claim: Dorsal nIII subnuclei expressed cdh10a (type II), which exhibited negligible expression in ventromedial nIII.
source: Dorsal subnuclei expressed several cadherins, including cdh4 (type I; Figure 1E, I and L) and cdh10a (type II; Figure 1G, K and L), which exhibited negligible expression in ventromedial nIII.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAscope data shown in Figure 1G, K and L.

claim: Expression of cdh8 (type II) was far higher in ventral than in dorsal nIII at 48 hpf.
source: In contrast, other cadherins were robustly expressed by all nIII neurons, but to varying degrees: expression of cdh8 (type II; Figure 1F, J and L; Video 1) was far higher in ventral than in dorsal nIII, whereas cdh7a expression (type II; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, F and L; Video 2) was lower in ventral neurons compared to dorsolateral nIII neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAscope data shown in Figure 1F, J and L and Video 1.

claim: cdh7a expression (type II) was lower in ventral neurons compared to dorsolateral nIII neurons at 48 hpf.
source: In contrast, other cadherins were robustly expressed by all nIII neurons, but to varying degrees: expression of cdh8 (type II; Figure 1F, J and L; Video 1) was far higher in ventral than in dorsal nIII, whereas cdh7a expression (type II; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, F and L; Video 2) was lower in ventral neurons compared to dorsolateral nIII neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAscope data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, F and L and Video 2.

claim: Differences in cadherin expression were observed between dorsolateral and dorsomedial domains for some cadherins, including cdh7a and cdh8, although these tended to be smaller than those observed between dorsal and ventral domains.
source: In addition, we observed differences between dorsolateral and dorsomedial domains for some cadherins, including cdh7a and cdh8, although these tended to be smaller than those observed between dorsal and ventral domains (Figure 1L).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: At 72 hpf, ocular motor neurons continued to express cadherin combinations.
source: At 72 hpf, ocular motor neurons continued to express cadherin combinations (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), with continued broad CNS expression of cdh11 and cdh2;
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAscope data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: cdh2 continued to be the most highly expressed cadherin across both nuclei at 72 hpf.
source: At 72 hpf, ocular motor neurons continued to express cadherin combinations (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), with continued broad CNS expression of cdh11 and cdh2; cdh2 continued to be the most highly expressed cadherin across both nuclei (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C, J and Q).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C, J and Q.

claim: Several cadherins showed higher overall expression in nIII at 72 hpf compared to 48 hpf, most notably cdh4 and cdh13.
source: Several cadherins showed higher overall expression in nIII compared to 48 hpf, most notably cdh4 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D, K and Q) and cdh13 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3I, P and Q).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Differential expression of cadherins between dorsal and ventral nIII was maintained at 72 hpf.
source: Despite this, differential expression between dorsal and ventral nIII was maintained: expression of cdh10a remained absent from the most medial part of ventromedial nIII, resulting in lower levels of expression compared to dorsolateral nIII (Figure 1—figure supplement 3G, N and Q), whereas expression of cdh8 was higher compared to dorsal nIII (Figure 1—figure supplement 3F, M and Q).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Dorsal and ventral ocular motor subnuclei are defined by unique combinations of cadherin expression during the timeframe of nucleogenesis.
source: These results reveal a complex organisation of cadherin expression in developing ocular motor neurons, whereby dorsal and ventral ocular motor subnuclei are defined by unique combinations of cadherin expression during the timeframe of nucleogenesis, and point to a role for both type I and type II cadherins in their development.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the RNAscope expression data presented in Figure 1 and supplements.

claim: The cdh2ΔEC construct carries a large deletion encompassing ectodomains 1–4 of cdh2.
source: This construct (cdh2ΔEC) carries a large deletion encompassing ectodomains 1–4 of cdh2, and blocks cadherin adhesive function in an isotype-nonspecific manner, causing non-adhesive phenotypes in cells in which it is overexpressed by occupying sites where endogenous cadherins would otherwise localise, as well as by facilitating their endocytosis (Rebman et al., 2016; Kintner, 1992; Nieman et al., 1999; Jontes et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations describing the construct.

claim: The cdh2ΔEC construct blocks cadherin adhesive function in an isotype-nonspecific manner.
source: This construct (cdh2ΔEC) carries a large deletion encompassing ectodomains 1–4 of cdh2, and blocks cadherin adhesive function in an isotype-nonspecific manner, causing non-adhesive phenotypes in cells in which it is overexpressed by occupying sites where endogenous cadherins would otherwise localise, as well as by facilitating their endocytosis (Rebman et al., 2016; Kintner, 1992; Nieman et al., 1999; Jontes et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations describing the mechanism of action.

claim: The cdh2ΔEC construct is expected to perturb both type I and type II cadherin-mediated adhesion.
source: As a result, it is expected to perturb both type I and type II cadherin-mediated adhesion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the non-specific mechanism of the dominant negative construct.

claim: Both nIII and nIV are complete in terms of absolute numbers of terminally differentiated neurons at 72 hpf.
source: In order to examine the effect of perturbing cadherin function on the organisation of ocular motor neurons, we performed live imaging of wild-type Isl1:GFP and cdh2ΔEC larvae at 72 hpf (Figure 2), when both nIII and nIV are complete in terms of absolute numbers of terminally differentiated neurons and have also innervated their appropriate muscle targets during normal development.
evidence: This is a statement about the developmental stage chosen for analysis.

claim: Both nIII and nIV have innervated their appropriate muscle targets at 72 hpf during normal development.
source: In order to examine the effect of perturbing cadherin function on the organisation of ocular motor neurons, we performed live imaging of wild-type Isl1:GFP and cdh2ΔEC larvae at 72 hpf (Figure 2), when both nIII and nIV are complete in terms of absolute numbers of terminally differentiated neurons and have also innervated their appropriate muscle targets during normal development.
evidence: This is a statement about the developmental stage chosen for analysis.

claim: Live imaging revealed expression of cdh2ΔEC in all GFP-positive nIII neurons.
source: Live imaging revealed expression of cdh2ΔEC, as evidenced by punctate mCherry-positive fluorescence, in all GFP-positive nIII neurons, however no signal was observed in adjacent GFP-negative IO neurons, nVI neurons or other surrounding cell types, recapitulating the lack of expression observed in Isl1:GFP (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: No cdh2ΔEC signal was observed in adjacent GFP-negative IO neurons, nVI neurons or other surrounding cell types.
source: Live imaging revealed expression of cdh2ΔEC, as evidenced by punctate mCherry-positive fluorescence, in all GFP-positive nIII neurons, however no signal was observed in adjacent GFP-negative IO neurons, nVI neurons or other surrounding cell types, recapitulating the lack of expression observed in Isl1:GFP (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Following perturbation of cadherin function, dorsal and ventral nIII populations were still visibly distinct as in wild types.
source: Following perturbation of cadherin function, dorsal and ventral nIII populations were still visibly distinct as in wild types (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), however the positioning of dorsal nIII neurons was perturbed (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2B.

claim: The positioning of dorsal nIII neurons was perturbed following perturbation of cadherin function.
source: Following perturbation of cadherin function, dorsal and ventral nIII populations were still visibly distinct as in wild types (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), however the positioning of dorsal nIII neurons was perturbed (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In cdh2ΔEC larvae, dorsal nIII neurons were more sparsely distributed than their wild-type counterparts.
source: Two main phenotypes were observed: Firstly, neurons were more sparsely distributed than their wild-type counterparts (Figure 2C–D').
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2C–D'.

claim: In cdh2ΔEC larvae, dorsal nIII neurons were often scattered over a wider area, so that occasionally small groups of dorsal cells were found clustered a greater distance away from the rest of the nucleus.
source: Secondly, they were often also scattered over a wider area, so that occasionally small groups of dorsal cells were found clustered a greater distance away from the rest of the nucleus (Figure 2E–E').
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2E–E'.

claim: The density and positioning of neurons located in ventromedial nIII was not perturbed in cdh2ΔEC larvae.
source: Interestingly, the density and positioning of neurons located in ventromedial nIII was not perturbed.
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data.

claim: The number of cells measured per side, per larva did not differ depending on the genotype.
source: The number of cells measured per side, per larva did not differ depending on the genotype (Figure 2G), suggesting that normal programmes of differentiation were unlikely to be affected following perturbation of cadherin function, recapitulating previous findings (Astick et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2G and a citation to Astick et al., 2014.

claim: Normal programmes of differentiation were unlikely to be affected following perturbation of cadherin function.
source: The number of cells measured per side, per larva did not differ depending on the genotype (Figure 2G), suggesting that normal programmes of differentiation were unlikely to be affected following perturbation of cadherin function, recapitulating previous findings (Astick et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on cell count data and supported by a citation.

claim: There was a significant increase in the convex hull volumes of dorsal nIII neurons in cdh2ΔEC larvae.
source: However, there was a significant increase in the convex hull volumes (the volume of the smallest convex set in Euclidean space containing all coordinates) of dorsal nIII neurons in cdh2ΔEC larvae (Figure 2F), demonstrating that these neurons occupy a larger area in 3D space as a result of disrupted cadherin function.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Dorsal nIII neurons occupy a larger area in 3D space in cdh2ΔEC larvae as a result of disrupted cadherin function.
source: However, there was a significant increase in the convex hull volumes (the volume of the smallest convex set in Euclidean space containing all coordinates) of dorsal nIII neurons in cdh2ΔEC larvae (Figure 2F), demonstrating that these neurons occupy a larger area in 3D space as a result of disrupted cadherin function.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the convex hull volume data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Local cell densities estimated by Delaunay tessellation were significantly reduced in cdh2ΔEC larvae compared to wild types.
source: Furthermore, local cell densities estimated by Delaunay tessellation were significantly reduced in these larvae compared to wild types (Figure 2G), indicating that, overall, cdh2ΔEC-expressing neurons in dorsal nIII have fewer oculomotor neighbours as a result of weakened adhesions.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: cdh2ΔEC-expressing neurons in dorsal nIII have fewer oculomotor neighbours as a result of weakened adhesions.
source: Furthermore, local cell densities estimated by Delaunay tessellation were significantly reduced in these larvae compared to wild types (Figure 2G), indicating that, overall, cdh2ΔEC-expressing neurons in dorsal nIII have fewer oculomotor neighbours as a result of weakened adhesions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the local cell density data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Cadherins are required for the clustering and correct positioning of IR/MR subnuclei of nIII.
source: We conclude that cadherins are required for the clustering and correct positioning of IR/MR subnuclei of nIII.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: In the developing CNS, contralateral connectivity is predominantly established via midline-crossing commissural axons, which are guided by axon guidance factors secreted by midline cells.
source: In the developing CNS, contralateral connectivity is predominantly established via midline-crossing commissural axons, which are guided by axon guidance factors secreted by midline cells (Ypsilanti et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ypsilanti et al., 2010.

claim: The contralateral innervation pattern of superior rectus (SR) neurons is the product of an unusual and well-conserved migration during which they translocate their soma across the midline to the contralateral side.
source: In contrast, the contralateral innervation pattern of superior rectus (SR) neurons, which are located in ventral nIII, is the product of an unusual and well-conserved migration during which they translocate their soma across the midline to the contralateral side (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a description of the unique migration pattern of SR neurons.

claim: Studies in other vertebrates have shown that SR neurons send out axons ipsilaterally and migrate to the contralateral side along a leading process which extends into the contralateral nucleus, resulting in contralateral projection.
source: Studies in other vertebrates have shown that SR neurons send out axons ipsilaterally and migrate to the contralateral side along a leading process which extends into the contralateral nucleus, resulting in contralateral projection (Puelles-Lopez et al., 1975; Bjorke et al., 2016; Dun et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies in other vertebrates.

claim: Using live time-lapse imaging of wild-type Isl1:GFP embryos, bilateral ventral nIII neurons are initially separated at ~43.5 hpf and progressively converge towards the midline, until cells of either side are in contact from ~47 hpf.
source: Using live time-lapse imaging of wild-type Isl1:GFP embryos, we found that bilateral ventral nIII neurons are initially separated at ~43.5 hpf and progressively converge towards the midline, until cells of either side are in contact from ~47 hpf.
evidence: This claim is supported by live time-lapse imaging data.

claim: Ventral nIII neurons are found interdigitated at the midline by 72 hpf, suggesting that migration is underway.
source: Using immunohistochemistry against GFP in order to examine their arrangement, we found that ventral nIII neurons are found interdigitated at the midline by 72 hpf, suggesting that migration is underway (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: SR neuron migration is estimated to be complete by ~4 dpf based on contralateral cells counts following unilateral application of DiI to the orbit of fixed Isl1:GFP embryos of various developmental stages.
source: We estimate that SR neuron migration is complete by ~4 dpf based on contralateral cells counts following unilateral application of DiI to the orbit of fixed Isl1:GFP embryos of various developmental stages, (data not shown).
evidence: This is an estimate based on unpublished data.

claim: Wild-type ventral nIII neurons were found fully interdigitated at the midline in the majority of embryos at 50 hpf.
source: Whereas wild-type ventral nIII neurons were found fully interdigitated at the midline in the majority of embryos (Figure 3C), only a few cdh2ΔEC-expressing neurons had successfully converged, leaving a gap between large numbers of cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In cdh2ΔEC embryos at 50 hpf, only a few neurons had successfully converged at the midline, leaving a gap between large numbers of cells.
source: Whereas wild-type ventral nIII neurons were found fully interdigitated at the midline in the majority of embryos (Figure 3C), only a few cdh2ΔEC-expressing neurons had successfully converged, leaving a gap between large numbers of cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: There was a significant decrease in the area of GFP fluorescence at the midline in cdh2ΔEC embryos compared to wild types at 50 hpf.
source: There was a significant decrease in the area of GFP fluorescence imaged in cdh2ΔEC embryos (Figure 3F and G) compared to wild types (Figure 3E), whereas no difference was detected in the total numbers of nIII neurons between them.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3F and G.

claim: No difference was detected in the total numbers of nIII neurons between wild-type and cdh2ΔEC embryos at 50 hpf.
source: There was a significant decrease in the area of GFP fluorescence imaged in cdh2ΔEC embryos (Figure 3F and G) compared to wild types (Figure 3E), whereas no difference was detected in the total numbers of nIII neurons between them.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell count data.

claim: The convergence of SR neurons towards the midline is perturbed in cdh2ΔEC embryos, which is unlikely to be due to delayed neurogenesis.
source: This suggests that the convergence of SR neurons towards the midline is perturbed in cdh2ΔEC embryos, which is unlikely to be due to delayed neurogenesis.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the midline convergence data and cell count data.

claim: Live imaging experiments at 72 hpf show that cdh2ΔEC-expressing SR neurons eventually reach the midline.
source: Interestingly, our live imaging experiments at 72 hpf show that cdh2ΔEC-expressing SR neurons eventually reach the midline (Figure 2B and D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2B and D–E.

claim: Perturbing cadherin function delays, but does not prevent, the convergence of SR neurons towards the midline.
source: Overall, these results indicate that perturbing cadherin function delays, but does not prevent, the convergence of SR neurons towards the midline.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the temporal analysis of SR neuron convergence.

claim: Using unilateral application of DiI to the oculomotor nerve of fixed larvae at 5 dpf, groups of contralateral oculomotor neurons were labelled in wild types.
source: Using unilateral application of DiI to the oculomotor nerve of fixed larvae at 5 dpf, we labelled groups of contralateral oculomotor neurons in wild types (Figure 3I–I'); however, in cdh2ΔEC larvae, nIII-labelled neurons were only found on the ipsilateral side (Figure 3J–J'), suggesting that contralateral migration is abolished following the loss of cadherin adhesion.
evidence: This claim is supported by DiI labeling data shown in Figure 3I–I'.

claim: In cdh2ΔEC larvae at 5 dpf, nIII-labelled neurons were only found on the ipsilateral side.
source: Using unilateral application of DiI to the oculomotor nerve of fixed larvae at 5 dpf, we labelled groups of contralateral oculomotor neurons in wild types (Figure 3I–I'); however, in cdh2ΔEC larvae, nIII-labelled neurons were only found on the ipsilateral side (Figure 3J–J'), suggesting that contralateral migration is abolished following the loss of cadherin adhesion.
evidence: This claim is supported by DiI labeling data shown in Figure 3J–J'.

claim: Contralateral migration is abolished following the loss of cadherin adhesion.
source: Using unilateral application of DiI to the oculomotor nerve of fixed larvae at 5 dpf, we labelled groups of contralateral oculomotor neurons in wild types (Figure 3I–I'); however, in cdh2ΔEC larvae, nIII-labelled neurons were only found on the ipsilateral side (Figure 3J–J'), suggesting that contralateral migration is abolished following the loss of cadherin adhesion.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DiI labeling data.

claim: There was a dramatic reduction in the number of contralateral cells labelled in cdh2ΔEC larvae using sparse retro-orbital dye fills at 5 dpf.
source: Live imaging revealed dye-filled GFP-positive (SR) cells on the contralateral side in wild types (Figure 3K–K''), whereas there was a dramatic reduction in the number of contralateral cells labelled in cdh2ΔEC larvae, despite successful labelling of ipsilateral neurons (Figure 3L–L'').
evidence: This claim is supported by sparse labeling data shown in Figure 3K–L''.

claim: There was a significant relationship between genotype and subnuclear identity in retro-orbital dye fill experiments.
source: Examination of the pooled data revealed a significant relationship between genotype and subnuclear identity (Figure 3M).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3M.

claim: There was a significant reduction in the proportion of contralateral GFP-positive nIII cells in cdh2ΔEC larvae compared to wild types.
source: There was a significant reduction in the proportion of contralateral GFP-positive nIII cells in cdh2ΔEC larvae compared to wild types (Figure 3N), with 15/16 larvae exhibiting proportions of <5% of labelled SR neurons compared with 10/15 wild-type larvae, which had proportions of >5% ranging up to 65%.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3N.

claim: There was a significant increase in the proportion of ipsilateral GFP-positive cells in cdh2ΔEC larvae.
source: Indeed, there was a significant increase in the proportion of ipsilateral GFP-positive cells in cdh2ΔEC larvae (Figure 3O), which likely reflects the additional detection of SR neurons which have failed to migrate to the contralateral side, in addition to IR/MR cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3O.

claim: The increase in the proportion of ipsilateral GFP-positive cells in cdh2ΔEC larvae likely reflects the additional detection of SR neurons which have failed to migrate to the contralateral side, in addition to IR/MR cells.
source: Indeed, there was a significant increase in the proportion of ipsilateral GFP-positive cells in cdh2ΔEC larvae (Figure 3O), which likely reflects the additional detection of SR neurons which have failed to migrate to the contralateral side, in addition to IR/MR cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the quantitative data shown in Figure 3O.

claim: There was no difference in the proportions of dye-filled IO neurons between wild-type and cdh2ΔEC larvae.
source: In contrast, we found no difference in the proportions of dye-filled IO (Figure 3P) or SO/nIV neurons between genotypes (Figure 3Q).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3P.

claim: There was no difference in the proportions of dye-filled SO/nIV neurons between wild-type and cdh2ΔEC larvae.
source: In contrast, we found no difference in the proportions of dye-filled IO (Figure 3P) or SO/nIV neurons between genotypes (Figure 3Q).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3Q.

claim: The contralateral migration of SR neurons depends on cadherin-mediated adhesion.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that the contralateral migration of SR neurons depends on cadherin-mediated adhesion.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: SR neurons with perturbed cadherin adhesivity eventually reach the midline, but do not cross it.
source: Our finding that SR neurons with perturbed cadherin adhesivity eventually reach the midline, but do not cross it, suggests that contralateral migration proceeds via a two-phase process: an initial convergence towards the midline, followed by somal translocation across it.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the temporal analysis of SR neuron migration.

claim: Contralateral migration proceeds via a two-phase process: an initial convergence towards the midline, followed by somal translocation across it.
source: Our finding that SR neurons with perturbed cadherin adhesivity eventually reach the midline, but do not cross it, suggests that contralateral migration proceeds via a two-phase process: an initial convergence towards the midline, followed by somal translocation across it.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that SR neurons reach but do not cross the midline in cdh2ΔEC larvae.

claim: Although nIV neurons were not scattered in cdh2ΔEC larvae, they were aberrantly positioned along the DV axis, resulting in a significantly dorsally elongated trochlear nucleus compared to wild-type fish.
source: Interestingly, although nIV neurons were not scattered, they were aberrantly positioned along the DV axis, resulting in a significantly dorsally elongated trochlear nucleus compared to wild-type fish (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantitative data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The position of nIV did not appear to be shifted overall with respect to nIII in cdh2ΔEC larvae.
source: The position of nIV did not appear to be shifted overall with respect to nIII.
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data.

claim: During wild-type development, nIV elongates along the DV axis between 48hpf and 72hpf.
source: During wild-type development, nIV elongates along the DV axis between 48hpf and 72hpf (unpublished data), suggesting the presence of guidance cues or mechanical forces which act along this axis.
evidence: This claim is based on unpublished observations.

claim: Abrogating cadherin function in nIV neurons impairs the cohesion of the nucleus, resulting in its increased elongation.
source: We speculate that abrogating cadherin function in these neurons impairs the cohesion of the nucleus, resulting in its increased elongation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the nIV elongation phenotype.

claim: In cdh2ΔEC embryos, neurons belonging to the inferior oblique (IO) nucleus were never seen to express cdh2ΔEC-mCherry.
source: In cdh2ΔEC embryos, neurons belonging to the inferior oblique (IO) nucleus were never seen to express cdh2ΔEC-mCherry, allowing us to ask whether their position is dependent on cadherin function in other subnuclei.
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data.

claim: Several cadherins, including cdh2 and cdh11, are expressed by all oculomotor neurons, including IO neurons.
source: Several cadherins, including cdh2 and cdh11, are expressed by all oculomotor neurons, including IO neurons, whereas other type II cadherins which are capable of interacting heterophilically with cdh11, such as cdh8, are expressed differentially by subnuclei (Figure 1B–C; Brasch et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAscope data in Figure 1B–C and a citation to Brasch et al., 2018.

claim: Type II cadherins such as cdh8 are capable of interacting heterophilically with cdh11.
source: Several cadherins, including cdh2 and cdh11, are expressed by all oculomotor neurons, including IO neurons, whereas other type II cadherins which are capable of interacting heterophilically with cdh11, such as cdh8, are expressed differentially by subnuclei (Figure 1B–C; Brasch et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brasch et al., 2018.

claim: Homophilic and heterophilic cadherin-mediated adhesive interactions could arise between IO neurons and other oculomotor neurons.
source: This raises the possibility that homophilic and heterophilic cadherin-mediated adhesive interactions could arise between IO neurons and other oculomotor neurons.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the cadherin expression patterns.

claim: 3D-visualisation of nIII revealed that the IO subnucleus resembles a columnar organisation along the DV axis, with neurons located ventral and lateral to SR neurons, as well as dorsally and medially.
source: 3D-visualisation of nIII revealed that the IO subnucleus resembles a columnar organisation along the DV axis, with neurons located ventral and lateral to SR neurons, as well as dorsally and medially (Figure 5A–A'').
evidence: This claim is supported by 3D visualization data shown in Figure 5A–A''.

claim: The overall cellular distribution for IO neurons was significantly different between wild-type and cdh2ΔEC genotypes.
source: We first assessed differences in the distribution of IO neuron location using a multivariate extension of the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. This revealed that the overall cellular distribution for IO neurons was significantly different between genotypes (k = 0.2427, p<0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: In wild types, probabilities of IO location are biased towards medial locations and are found along the DV axis, with slightly higher probabilities for dorsal regions.
source: In wild types, probabilities of IO location are biased towards medial locations and are found along the DV axis, with slightly higher probabilities for dorsal regions (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by probability distribution data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In cdh2ΔEC larvae, reduced dorsal and slightly more lateral probabilities were observed for IO neurons.
source: In cdh2ΔEC larvae, reduced dorsal and slightly more lateral probabilities were observed for IO neurons (Figure 5C–D); however, the overall arrangement of IO neurons as a subnucleus appeared similar.
evidence: This claim is supported by probability distribution data shown in Figure 5C–D.

claim: The overall arrangement of IO neurons as a subnucleus appeared similar between wild-type and cdh2ΔEC larvae.
source: In cdh2ΔEC larvae, reduced dorsal and slightly more lateral probabilities were observed for IO neurons (Figure 5C–D); however, the overall arrangement of IO neurons as a subnucleus appeared similar.
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data.

claim: Estimated DV-ML occupancy distributions confirmed differences in the overall spatial distribution of IO neurons between genotypes.
source: Estimated DV-ML occupancy distributions confirmed differences in the overall spatial distribution of IO neurons between genotypes (Figure 5E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian analysis shown in Figure 5E–G.

claim: There was an overall tendency towards higher, dorsal values for DV subdivision in wild types compared to cdh2ΔEC larvae.
source: We investigated the directionality of the shift along the two major axes and found an overall tendency towards higher, dorsal values for DV subdivision in wild types compared to cdh2ΔEC larvae (Figure 5H).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5H.

claim: There was a slight tendency overall to lower, medial values for wild types compared to cdh2ΔEC larvae.
source: Additionally, there was a slight tendency overall to lower, medial values for wild types (Figure 5I).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5I.

claim: The positioning of IO neurons of cdh2ΔEC larvae is altered compared to wild types: IO neurons are located more ventral and lateral, consistent with a shift away from adjacent IR/MR and SR subnuclei.
source: This demonstrates that overall, the positioning of IO neurons of cdh2ΔEC larvae is altered compared to wild types: IO neurons are located more ventral and lateral, consistent with a shift away from adjacent IR/MR and SR subnuclei (Figure 5J–K).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the spatial distribution analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Cadherin-dependent neuron-neuron adhesive interactions between oculomotor subnuclei contribute to the appropriate positioning of the IO subnucleus.
source: In sum, these results suggest that cadherin-dependent neuron-neuron adhesive interactions between oculomotor subnuclei also contribute to the appropriate positioning of the IO subnucleus.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the IO positioning data in Figure 5.

claim: The observed shift in IO subnucleus position could be a mechanically driven consequence of changes to the arrangement of the other oculomotor subnuclei.
source: However, we cannot rule out an alternative possibility that the observed shift in IO subnucleus position could also be a mechanically driven consequence of changes to the arrangement of the other oculomotor subnuclei;
evidence: This is an alternative interpretation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: Some studies report that perturbations to cadherin signalling in hindbrain cranial motor neurons affect the positioning of soma, while preserving stereotyped patterns of axon outgrowth and pathfinding.
source: Whereas some studies report that perturbations to cadherin signalling in hindbrain cranial motor neurons affect the positioning of soma, while preserving stereotyped patterns of axon outgrowth and pathfinding (Astick et al., 2014; Rebman et al., 2016), others have identified a role for specific classical cadherins in the regulation of normal axonal development in motor neurons, including pathfinding, axon outgrowth and branching (Brusés, 2011; Barnes et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Other studies have identified a role for specific classical cadherins in the regulation of normal axonal development in motor neurons, including pathfinding, axon outgrowth and branching.
source: Whereas some studies report that perturbations to cadherin signalling in hindbrain cranial motor neurons affect the positioning of soma, while preserving stereotyped patterns of axon outgrowth and pathfinding (Astick et al., 2014; Rebman et al., 2016), others have identified a role for specific classical cadherins in the regulation of normal axonal development in motor neurons, including pathfinding, axon outgrowth and branching (Brusés, 2011; Barnes et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: At 72 hpf, all ocular motor nerves and branches were present and appeared to have reached their respective EOMs in cdh2ΔEC larvae.
source: At 72 hpf, all ocular motor nerves and branches were present and appeared to have reached their respective EOMs (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6A–B.

claim: There was no significant difference in the number of axon branches between wild-type and cdh2ΔEC genotypes.
source: There was no significant difference in the number of branches between genotypes (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Axon outgrowth, targeting and fasciculation of ocular motor axons is robust to cell-autonomous dominant negative cadherin expression.
source: These observations indicate that axon outgrowth, targeting and fasciculation of ocular motor axons is robust to cell-autonomous dominant negative cadherin expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the axon analysis data in Figure 6.

claim: Synaptogenesis is underway in all extraocular muscles from 72 hpf.
source: We have previously shown that synaptogenesis is underway in all muscles from 72 hpf (Clark et al., 2013), correlating with the onset of spontaneous saccadic eye movements (Easter and Nicola, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The onset of synaptogenesis correlates with the onset of spontaneous saccadic eye movements.
source: We have previously shown that synaptogenesis is underway in all muscles from 72 hpf (Clark et al., 2013), correlating with the onset of spontaneous saccadic eye movements (Easter and Nicola, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: cdh2 is known to localise at developing NMJs.
source: Cadherins have known roles in the formation of central synapses (reviewed in Salinas and Price, 2005) and cdh2 is known to localise at developing NMJs (Cifuentes-Diaz et al., 1994; Brusés, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Pre- and postsynaptic components colocalise as discrete patches on respective EOMs both in wild types and cdh2ΔEC larvae at 4 dpf.
source: We found that pre- and postsynaptic components colocalise as discrete patches on respective EOMs both in wild types and cdh2ΔEC larvae (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–H''), including on the medial rectus (MR) muscle (Figure 6D–G''), which is one of two muscles driving horizontal eye movements of the larval optokinetic reflex.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was no difference in the overall area of SV2 signal between wild-type and cdh2ΔEC larvae.
source: Furthermore, we observed no difference in the overall area of SV2 signal (Figure 6—figure supplement 1I) or degree of colocalisation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1J), suggesting that NMJs form properly following perturbation of cadherin adhesion.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1I.

claim: There was no difference in the degree of colocalisation of pre- and postsynaptic components between wild-type and cdh2ΔEC larvae.
source: Furthermore, we observed no difference in the overall area of SV2 signal (Figure 6—figure supplement 1I) or degree of colocalisation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1J), suggesting that NMJs form properly following perturbation of cadherin adhesion.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1J.

claim: NMJs form properly following perturbation of cadherin adhesion.
source: Furthermore, we observed no difference in the overall area of SV2 signal (Figure 6—figure supplement 1I) or degree of colocalisation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1J), suggesting that NMJs form properly following perturbation of cadherin adhesion.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the NMJ analysis data.

claim: Perturbing cadherin function does not erode the peripheral connection between ocular motor neurons and muscle targets.
source: Taken together, our findings suggest that perturbing cadherin function does not erode the peripheral connection between ocular motor neurons and muscle targets.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the axon and NMJ analysis data in Figure 6.

claim: The OKR is a well-conserved gaze-stabilising reflex which consists of slow-phase and fast reset eye movements in response to optic flow.
source: The OKR is a well-conserved gaze-stabilising reflex which consists of slow-phase and fast reset eye movements in response to optic flow.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the OKR.

claim: In zebrafish, the OKR is robust by 3–4 dpf.
source: In zebrafish, the OKR is robust by 3–4 dpf (Easter and Nicola, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Easter and Nicola, 1997.

claim: The horizontal eye movements of the OKR rely on the action of two antagonistic EOMs, the oculomotor-driven medial rectus and abducens nucleus-controlled lateral rectus.
source: The horizontal eye movements of the OKR rely on the action of two antagonistic EOMs, the oculomotor-driven medial rectus and abducens nucleus-controlled lateral rectus (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the neural control of the OKR.

claim: nVI neurons of cdh2ΔEC larvae do not express cdh2ΔEC.
source: As nVI neurons of cdh2ΔEC larvae do not express cdh2ΔEC, expression is restricted to MR neurons which are known to be contained within dorsal nIII and display a severely scattered phenotype in cdh2ΔEC larvae (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on the expression pattern of the transgene.

claim: MR neurons are known to be contained within dorsal nIII and display a severely scattered phenotype in cdh2ΔEC larvae.
source: As nVI neurons of cdh2ΔEC larvae do not express cdh2ΔEC, expression is restricted to MR neurons which are known to be contained within dorsal nIII and display a severely scattered phenotype in cdh2ΔEC larvae (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Cell-specific perturbation of cadherin function would primarily affect nasal rather than temporal eye movements.
source: We therefore hypothesised that cell-specific perturbation of cadherin function would primarily affect nasal rather than temporal eye movements.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the selective expression of cdh2ΔEC in MR neurons.

claim: cdh2ΔEC larvae displayed severe defects in the efficiency of their nasal eye movements when compared to wild types.
source: We found that cdh2ΔEC larvae displayed severe defects in the efficiency of their nasal eye movements when compared to wild types (Figure 7C), exhibiting a significant decrease in the eye gain for both eyes across all trials, with the strongest effect seen for the strong eye.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: cdh2ΔEC larvae exhibited a significant decrease in the eye gain for nasal movements for both eyes across all trials, with the strongest effect seen for the strong eye.
source: We found that cdh2ΔEC larvae displayed severe defects in the efficiency of their nasal eye movements when compared to wild types (Figure 7C), exhibiting a significant decrease in the eye gain for both eyes across all trials, with the strongest effect seen for the strong eye.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: There was no difference in the eye gain for temporal eye movements between cdh2ΔEC larvae and wild types for either strong or weak eyes.
source: Conversely, we found no difference in the eye gain for temporal eye movements between cdh2ΔEC larvae and wild types for either strong or weak eyes (Figure 7D), although variability was higher for cdh2ΔEC larvae.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Variability in temporal eye gain was higher for cdh2ΔEC larvae compared to wild types.
source: Conversely, we found no difference in the eye gain for temporal eye movements between cdh2ΔEC larvae and wild types for either strong or weak eyes (Figure 7D), although variability was higher for cdh2ΔEC larvae.
evidence: This is an observation from the quantitative data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: There was a significant decrease in the eye range of each eye in cdh2ΔEC larvae, with a more pronounced effect observed for the strong eye.
source: We also observed a significant decrease in the eye range of each eye in cdh2ΔEC larvae (Figure 7E), with a more pronounced effect observed for the strong eye.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The efficiency of nasal eye movements (mediated by the MR muscle) as well as overall range of movement is significantly impaired in larvae in which cadherin-mediated adhesion in oculomotor neurons is reduced.
source: Taken together, these data show that the efficiency of nasal eye movements (mediated by the MR muscle) as well as overall range of movement is significantly impaired in larvae in which cadherin-mediated adhesion in oculomotor neurons is reduced.
evidence: This is a summary of the behavioral data presented in Figure 7.

claim: The finding that the temporal eye movements of the OKR are not impaired is consistent with a specific effect of cdh2ΔEC expression on MR-driven motor control rather than visual impairment.
source: Our finding that the temporal eye movements of the OKR are not impaired is consistent with a specific effect of cdh2ΔEC expression on MR-driven motor control rather than visual impairment and suggests that the clustered arrangement of these neurons is important for the function of the motor circuit.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral data.

claim: The clustered arrangement of MR neurons is important for the function of the motor circuit.
source: Our finding that the temporal eye movements of the OKR are not impaired is consistent with a specific effect of cdh2ΔEC expression on MR-driven motor control rather than visual impairment and suggests that the clustered arrangement of these neurons is important for the function of the motor circuit.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between disrupted clustering and impaired motor function.

claim: Cadherin-based interactions likely coordinate the positioning of motor neurons both within and between subnuclei.
source: Our findings show that cadherin-based interactions likely coordinate the positioning of motor neurons both within and between subnuclei.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Dorsal nIII (IR/MR) and ventral (SR) neurons display differential positioning defects when cadherin function is disrupted in these subnuclei.
source: This is evidenced by the observations that dorsal nIII (IR/MR) and ventral (SR) neurons display differential positioning defects when cadherin function is disrupted in these subnuclei, and that the location of the adjacent IO subnucleus is shifted following this perturbation.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: The location of the adjacent IO subnucleus is shifted following perturbation of cadherin function in other subnuclei.
source: This is evidenced by the observations that dorsal nIII (IR/MR) and ventral (SR) neurons display differential positioning defects when cadherin function is disrupted in these subnuclei, and that the location of the adjacent IO subnucleus is shifted following this perturbation.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: It has previously been proposed that cadherins globally expressed by motor neurons provide a baseline level of adhesion, while selective expression of other cadherins facilitates their sorting into distinct nuclei.
source: It has previously been proposed that cadherins globally expressed by motor neurons provide a baseline level of adhesion, while selective expression of other cadherins facilitates their sorting into distinct nuclei (Demireva et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Demireva et al., 2011.

claim: Several cadherins, including cdh2 and cdh11, are expressed by all subnuclei, highlighting them as prime candidates to drive baseline levels of adhesion via homophilic interactions.
source: We find that several cadherins, including cdh2 and cdh11, are expressed by all subnuclei, highlighting them as prime candidates to drive baseline levels of adhesion via homophilic interactions.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the cadherin expression data.

claim: Heterophilic interactions between type II cadherins belonging to specificity groups, such as cdh8 and cdh11, could participate in motor neuron positioning, in collaboration with cdh2.
source: Recent work raises the possibility that heterophilic interactions between type II cadherins belonging to specificity groups, such as cdh8 (expressed to varying degrees by IR/MR and SR) and cdh11 (expressed by all ocular motor neurons), could also participate, in collaboration with cdh2 (Brasch et al., 2018; Dewitz et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent work.

claim: The clustering of dorsal nIII neurons requires cadherin adhesivity.
source: Although we find that that the clustering of dorsal nIII neurons requires cadherin adhesivity, as previously shown for other cranial motor nuclei (Astick et al., 2014), ventral SR neurons do not appear to depend on cadherin function in the same way – here cadherins regulate transmedial migration.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 2 and a citation to Astick et al., 2014.

claim: Ventral SR neurons do not appear to depend on cadherin function for clustering in the same way as dorsal neurons – here cadherins regulate transmedial migration.
source: Although we find that that the clustering of dorsal nIII neurons requires cadherin adhesivity, as previously shown for other cranial motor nuclei (Astick et al., 2014), ventral SR neurons do not appear to depend on cadherin function in the same way – here cadherins regulate transmedial migration.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differential phenotypes observed in Figure 2 and Figure 3.

claim: Dorsal nIII neurons, which are generated earlier and migrate dorsally, express additional cadherins during development.
source: Dorsal nIII neurons, which are generated earlier and migrate dorsally, express additional cadherins during development.
evidence: This claim is supported by the cadherin expression data in Figure 1.

claim: The coalescence of dorsal nIII neurons may be more cadherin-dependent because they express additional cadherins.
source: As such, their coalescence may be more cadherin-dependent.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the differential cadherin expression.

claim: Dorsal subnuclei differentially express several classical cadherins, including cdh4 and cdh10a.
source: In addition, dorsal subnuclei differentially express several classical cadherins, including cdh4 and cdh10a.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAscope data in Figure 1.

claim: SR-innervating oculomotor neurons are one of a small number of neuronal cell types known to complete transmedial migration during development.
source: SR-innervating oculomotor neurons are one of a small number of neuronal cell types known to complete transmedial migration during development (Simon and Lumsden, 1993; Taniguchi et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cadherins are one of the few molecular factors regulating the distinctive transmedial migration of SR neurons.
source: We identify cadherins as one of the few molecular factors regulating this distinctive migration.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: Cadherins facilitate the timely convergence of SR neurons towards the midline and are required for their subsequent ability to cross it.
source: Our analyses show that they facilitate the timely convergence of SR neurons towards the midline and are required for their subsequent ability to cross it, suggesting that contralateral migration occurs in two steps.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: Cadherins are known to contribute to cell migration by coupling to retrograde actin flow, thereby acting as a molecular clutch.
source: Cadherins are known to contribute to cell migration by coupling to retrograde actin flow, thereby acting as a molecular clutch (Bard et al., 2008; Garcia et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cadherins acting as a molecular clutch constitutes one possible mechanism by which cadherins facilitate the movement of SR neurons across the midline.
